en: Thus, the procedure for the fire oblation (homa) is now described.
"Whatever mantras are deficient or redundant that are always worshipped through fire-offerings (homa),
therefore the Vajradharas of the three supreme bodies praise the fire-offering."
All ritual actions and vidyās do not always produce results in the same way that fire-offerings (homas) bring about the unsurpassed accomplishment of rites.
Homas are said to be of many kinds, but in brief they are fivefold;
they will be explained in detail in the *Mahāyogaguhyatantra*.

I shall now briefly explain the miraculous transformations of the Vidyādharas, just as the family maṇḍala is accomplished through the ritual procedure of the fire offering (*homa*). (Note: This refers to the *Guhyatantra* as a Mahāyoga Tantra!)
The fire-offering rites are fivefold; thus, each one is extensive:
the pacifying (śāntika), the nourishing (pauṣṭika), and the third is the malevolent (abhicāruka).
The fourth is indeed attraction, and the fifth is established as subjugation;
these are the five rites, among which subjugation is the most excellent.
It is said that the characteristics of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) are indeed according to tradition,
beginning from one cubit up to a thousand cubits.
Indeed, this very measurement of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) applies to all rites;
however, for rites against enemies, one should make it eight finger-breadths larger than a cubit.
Ten fingers and so forth are for nourishment; twelve more [twelve] are for subjugation;
fourteen are for pacification; and sixteen are for the increase of the lineage.
An increase of eighteen finger-breadths brings prosperity to the location and the cowherd community;
by the addition of twenty finger-breadths, the pacification of the kingdom is ordained.
Having divided this measurement into three parts, one should dig two parts;
the eighth part of what has been dug is proclaimed to be the rim of the pit (kuṇḍa).
One should fashion the portion for the rim with half the measure of the lip;
with a measurement of eight finger-breadths, one should create an eight-petaled lotus.
Outside of that, one should indicate a vajra-fence measuring one finger-breadth;
in the central wheel, one should create an eight-petaled lotus measuring eight finger-breadths.
Having drawn a vajra in the center of that, measuring one finger-breadth,
the wise man should place a small disc within the triangular pit.
In the rite of sorcery (abhicāra), the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) for the fire-oblation (homakarma) should indeed be triangular;
one should dig it to half the depth of the pit's measurement.

For rites of pacification, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is said by those skilled in fire-offerings to be four-cornered; for rites of subjugation, it is circular; and for rites of nourishment, that same [shape] is prescribed.
For the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*), it is called the "half-moon," which is one-eighth the size of the rite of immobilization (*stambhana*);
the lip, however, is adorned with vajra symbols in its four locations.
One should place the splendor of the moon-vajra in the corners;
between the master’s fire-pit and [the other], one should construct a lofty Kailāsa.
One should specify the measurement in cubits by both length and circumference;
however, the span is measured by extension, and it should be provided with three steps.
Above that, having carefully drawn an eight-petaled lotus,
a vessel should be placed above the lotus at a distance of four finger-breadths, serving as a step.
And there, on one of the steps, the wise man should have a *sruva* ladle placed;
he should cause the eight symbols to be made upon the previously mentioned lotus petals.
One should produce the Maitreya-nāgapuṣpa for Kṣitigarbha,
the wheel for Vajrapāṇi, and the jewel for Khagarbha.
One should draw the lotus of the Lord of the World (Lokanātha), and the vajra of Mañjuśrī;
the sword is the emblem of Bhiṣkambhin, and one should depict the vajra of Bhadra. One should draw the emblems of the bodhisattvas in order, beginning from the east.
Such is the instruction.
What is the description of the sacrificial fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*)?
[It should be made from the wood] of the *palāśa*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, *kāśmarya*, *āmra*, *kadambaka*,
*śamī*, *plakṣa*, *vaṭa*, and trees growing in milky sap (*kṣīravṛkṣa*).
The tips of their respective pairs of stalks should be fresh, consisting of two leaves each,
and mixed with ghee, honey, curd, clarified butter, milk, and sugar-candy.
Anointed with the five nectars and fragrant substances, and bathed once again,
they are further made thick according to the measure of the little finger and provided with knots.
What is the *annasamacchidā*?
It is known to be twelve finger-breadths in length,
and its tips are considered to be free from the defects of being worn out, made of *aguru*, thin, long, or crooked.
Those [leaves] that are free from defects,
not eaten by insects, with their stalks and bark intact, and auspicious,
lead to the destruction of ignorance when short; whereas those that are split lead to disease, even if they appear beautiful.
What is remembered as *anne*?
That which is shattered brings about the destruction of water and causes misfortune. ...
[those] with mouths [turned] toward their place cause a fall from one's station; those with two tongues [cause] strife.
A woman who is stout causes quarrels; one who is emaciated brings about total destruction;
and one who is withered leads to the loss of fortune. Therefore, one should avoid these types of women.
Now, I shall briefly describe it by means of other substances:
namely, rice grains, grain known as *dhānya*, sesame seeds, cotton, and seeds.
What is the sacrificial food (*ājya*)? It consists of white mustard seeds, barley, wheat, and black gram, along with boiled rice mixed with curd;
specifically, it includes curd, milk, honey, parched grain flour, and parched rice.
One should fashion the wood known as *pañcakṣīra*, measuring fourteen finger-breadths, for rites of pacification (*śāntika*); it should be free from insects and wormholes.
In rites for nourishment (pauṣṭika), [the offerings] are known as black sesame, mung beans, rice, barley, and boiled rice;
as well as fragrance, saffron, milk, ghee, and māṣa-bean flour.
Especially by means of an oblation of *yejīna* soaked in ghee and milk;
thereafter, here, one should take wood from the five-milk trees, fourteen finger-breadths in length.
Having collected the fruit of *tikta*, *raktakuṇṭa*, *priyaṅgu*, and *nāgapuṣpa*, as well as *āsurī* and *natapuṣpikā*, [these are used] in the rite called subjugation (*vaśya*).
Vāsaka, devadāru, puṃnāga, and vaṭa, combined with honey and clarified butter, as well as the aforementioned wood; these [should be used].
Furthermore, the practitioner should offer oblations measuring twelve finger-breadths,
using black sesame seeds, mung beans, and the fruit of the bhallātaka tree.
Having stirred it with pungent oil, especially mixed with blood,
there is also the application of pungent *bhallātaka* and the fruit of *malūra*.
And for those two, dry wood measuring eight finger-breadths [is used] in the rite of malevolent magic (abhicārakarma).
In that ritual, one should mix the powder of mustard, mung beans, and black gram,
and stir it with red unbroken rice grains and pungent oil.
Furthermore, for the purpose of eradication (uccāṭana), the practitioner must always certainly offer as oblation wood from the *kāñcana* tree, and especially that of the *vāsaka*.
Fish, meats, grains, *kaṇikā*, barley, and beans—
all these types of rice must necessarily be red, black, or white.
One should also perform the rite of immobilization (stambhana) by offering oblations with a crow’s wing, its feathers, wood from a *danu* tree,
or even discarded wood.
The fuel sticks are from the Bodhi tree, along with five hundred fruits;
likewise, [offerings] of bilva fruit, curd, ghee, and honey.
Having stirred [the vessel], one should offer the oblation; it shall restore long-lost fortune.
For whomever's sake one performs this, one should visualize that person standing before oneself;
sprinkled with the glory of sovereignty, he shall duly obtain all prosperity.
I shall now explain the secret fire-sacrifice (*guhyahoma*) by which happiness is attained:
cow-flesh is prescribed for pacification (*śānti*), and elephant-flesh for immobilization (*stambhana*).
For incitement, camel meat is prescribed; likewise, for causing enmity, buffalo meat;
for killing, human flesh is declared; and for muteness, goat and ram meat.
In the rite for pacifying [illness], one should offer the meat of a ram;
in the rite for driving away [enemies], the meat of a donkey; in the rite for subduing, the meat of a hare;
and in the rite of attraction, one should likewise offer the meat of a *ṭiṭṭibha* bird, which grants success.
One should face the east for the purpose of pacification, and the north for nourishment;
facing the south, one should perform rites of sorcery.
One with an upward-turned face should perform the drawing-in [of the deity] by gazing in all directions;
one skilled in the ritual procedure should offer oblations facing west for the purpose of subjugation (*vaśya*).
In rites for pacification, the mark is the wheel; in rites for enrichment, the jewel-mudrā;
in rites for subjugation, it is known as the lotus; and in rites for killing, the vajra-krodha.
Vajrāṅkuśī should be understood as being for the purpose of attraction by those desiring results;
and by means of this fivefold yoga, the performance of the fire-offering (homa) rite is accomplished.
In rites of pacification, with a peaceful mind; in rites of enrichment, with an enriching mind;
in rites of subjugation, with an eager mind; and in rites of incitement, with a mind of distress.
But for the purpose of killing, one should have a cruel mind, be seated upon a harsh seat,
and have one's body covered with coarse blood-stained garments.
Either with his feet mounted upon the liṅga in his own lap, or else squatting,
he should press foot against foot and grind tooth against tooth.
On the fourteenth and eighth days of the dark fortnights, being angry with a frowning face,
one should perform the rite while seated in the wrathful posture (krodhaparyaṅka).
Whether one acts through the application of fierce anger or otherwise, at that time one should be seated on a high,
comfortable seat in the paryaṅka posture with a red-colored mind;
such are the characteristics of the directions prescribed for subjugation, nourishment, and attraction.
Thus ends the specification of the directions for the fuel-sticks and other materials.
The vessel may be made of copper or iron, or even of sacrificial wood, or even of neem wood;
and it should be shaped like a lotus petal.
It is said to be eight finger-breadths in length and four finger-breadths in width;
its center is depressed by two finger-breadths, and there too, it is marked with a vajra one finger-breadth [in size].
Furthermore, its staff shall consist of twenty-four finger-breadths according to the measurement of a well-proportioned man;
the fist, however, shall be four finger-breadths.
Above it is a row of tridents and vajras; the little finger serves as the channel-tube, or it may be four-cornered and very beautiful, measuring the length of the thumb.
Below the handle of the vajra-jewel is a parasol measuring one *gula*;
having carved an eight-petaled lotus, there is likewise a jewel above the lotus.
Alternatively, one should fashion a *makara* (sea-monster) beneath the bowl, adorned with lotuses;
its handle should be as thick as a closed fist, with a lotus at the base of the handle.

A vessel of such a kind would be the *śruva*; its characteristics are now described: it should be made of gold or other [precious materials], fashioned according to the prescribed method, and possess the appropriate measurements.
The measure of two thumb-breadths for the vessel and all its characteristics are described as being like those of the *tuḍujya*;
however, in the absence of the vessel and the *srū* ladle, it is performed by employing all the fingers.
One should properly offer the *pūrṇāhuti* with a three-fingered span reaching this goal;
or else, having prepared a tuft of hair from the root of a Bodhi tree or similar tree,
the teachers who are experts in the rules say that one should offer the oblation.
The specification of the *pātrī* and *sruva* ladles.
Since the vajra and bell are constituent parts of the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) and so forth in this context,
their characteristics are here described according to the Pīṭha-tantras.
Furthermore,
it should be fashioned from gold, copper, brass, or bell-metal;
its length and circumference should be proportionate to one's strength and capacity.
In that regard, the three-part vajra has ten spokes and consists of two parts;
the middle part, however, is the fist, which is explained in detail as follows.
There are five spokes, which are the five Buddhas; Vairocana is considered to be in the center, while Akṣobhya and the other Tathāgatas are in the spokes starting from the east.
Needles emerging from the mouths of sea-monsters have four, three, or more points;
they are shaped like buds or blue lotuses and are situated within moon-maṇḍalas.
Below that is an eight-petalled lotus, upon which are the eight sons of the Victors;
their emblems or seed-syllables are now described here.
For Padmapāṇi it is called the lotus; for Maitreya, the nāgapuṣpa flower;
and the emblem of Gaganagañjin is a jewel above the sky.
The vajra is the emblem of Bhadra, the lord of yakṣas; the sword is that of Mañjusvara; the staff is the sign of Bhiṣkambhin; and the wheel is held to be the mark of Kṣitigarbha.
The Praṇava is the seed-syllable of Padmapāṇi, and Maiṃ is that of Ajita;
Oṃkṛti is the seed-syllable of Gaganagañja, and the first letter of one's name is the seed-syllable of Bhadra.
One should produce the syllable *praṇava* for Vajrapāṇi, and *hūṃ* for Mañjuśrī; likewise, the *praṇava* for Bhaiṣajyasamudgata and the syllable *kṣāṃ* for Kṣitigarbha.
The seed-syllable or even a symbol should be placed on the petals starting from the east;
there should be eight petals as limbs, and in the center, the form of an egg.
There, Vairocana is seated in the abode of the thirty-three gods;
below that, upon an eight-petalled lotus, are the goddesses of knowledge in their respective order.
Vajrāṅkuśī, Pāśī, Sphoṭī, and Tārā are in the cardinal directions;
Cundā is in the intermediate directions, while Ratnolkā, Śṛṅkhalā, and Aparājitā are likewise situated.
Their sign is well-known, or else it is simply the first letter of their name;
this has been stated in the *Kramaśūkāḥ*, and [the signs] of the Vajra-women will now be described.
Vajraḍākī should be in the east, Ghorāḍākinī in the north;
Vettālī is in the west, and Caṇḍālī is recorded in the south.
Furthermore, the Jñāna-Ḍākinī should be known to have a medium-sized awn;
the four needles are considered to be progressively thicker, thicker, and with tips that diminish.
The middle finger is sharp, with its tip directed toward the [other fingers], having a pure middle joint like the belly of a barley grain;
furthermore, it is short and similar in shape to the others.
The ring finger is considered to be square, gradually tapering, and sharp;
this is the arrangement of the characteristics of the vajra.
The bell should be three parts [in height], and its handle one part;
the *bherī* drum is in the middle of that, with its opening having a width and length equal to the space between them.
In the center of that, one should contemplate the [deity] called Jñānadaṇḍa, the cause of creation and dissolution;
and in the directions such as the east and so forth, one should contemplate these deities.
Tārā is to be visualized in the eastern direction, and Pāṇḍarā should be in the north;
Māmakī is renowned in the west, and Locanā is considered to be in the south.
Vasudhārā, Cundā, Bhṛkuṭī, and Vajramālikā—these goddesses are to be known as being in the corners; their symbols and seed-syllables follow [their respective] directions.
Adorned with necklaces, half-necklaces, the moon, the sun, and two rows of vajras,
that center is indeed the middle of emptiness, having the nature of the realm of form.
But the pure formless realm is a blossomed, pure utpala lotus;
above that, one should place a golden or other-colored flask situated in the center of a pure moon.
Then, [one should visualize] the pure face of wisdom, filled with the liquid of nectar and possessing shaken fruits and sprouts, which is the arising of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
The beauty of form consists of the arrangement of the seed-syllables and the emblems of the previously mentioned deities upon the excellent petals;
then, from the second portion, there is the vajra with all its forms as before.
The bell may have a face like a budding lotus, or it may be shaped like a cow’s mouth;
having fashioned the *kamalāvarta* in five ways, one should place it in the eight directions.
One should perform the sounding of the bell, filling the sky with its resonance;
[visualizing] the moon, the crocodile, the seed-syllable, the sun, and indeed the right [side].
With his self being the union with his own chosen deity, he should sing the *hūṃ* syllable;
brandishing the vajra upward, he should delight all the Buddhas through the application of the bell and vajra according to the ritual of wisdom and means.

The Vajra is adorned; the *ullāla* is the liberation of the seven. Dharma is the supreme object in liberation; the Vajra indeed bears its shadow. *Oṃ vajraghaṇṭe hūṃ hoḥ*. *Oṃ vajraghaṇṭe raṇite praraṇite sarvabuddhapracālite prajñāpāramitānādasvabhāve vajradharahṛdayāvatoṣaṇi hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hoḥ hoḥ hoḥ aḥ aḥ aḥ svāhā*.
One should grasp the vajra with its true essence and ring the bell according to the Dharma;
through the union of wisdom and means, the practitioner fulfills the welfare of sentient beings.
But for one who is intent on ringing the bell through a practice that lacks reality, there will be no attainment of the desired goal; like the bell of an elephant, it does not sound.
The Summary of the Bell.
The fire offering (homa) is now described.
Having received the Agnihotra and other fires from the best of the twice-born for the sake of pacification,
as well as the consecrated homa-fire of those who have maintained the sacred fires, even by means of churning the two kindling woods (araṇi).
For nourishment, one should take fire from the kitchen of the Saṅgha or even from a fire-drill;
for killing, however, one should take it from the house of a king or a kṣatriya.
A funeral pyre of human bones is auspicious for subjugation; likewise is fire arising from a *caṇḍāla*’s house, or fire situated in a courtesan’s dwelling, or again, fire produced by a traveler.
In the rite of attraction, that which is born of the actor is also certain for fire-rites;
this must be understood with effort by the practitioner established in the tantra.
The section on the fire.
Then, having placed the fire upon dry grass in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and having sprinkled it with clarified butter (ghṛta), one should kindle it with fans and other means.
Oṃ jvala 2 hūṃ phaṭ!
Then, having gathered the *siddhārtha* seeds, either one hundred or twenty-eight times,
he should consecrate them with the mantra of Vighnāntaka while facing the ten directions.
Having recited [the mantra] and cast it into the center of the fire-pit, the knower of mantras, having dispelled the obstacles,
should extend his left hand and wave it while endowed with meditative visualization.
Oṃ hana 2 vajrakrodhe hūṃ.
The mantra for purifying the fire.
One should meditate upon the Fire-god within the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), seated upon a lotus throne,
with a mass of matted hair of tawny color, resembling molasses in luster, and holding a rosary of beads.
One should worship with objects of worship the deity born from the seed-syllable *rūṃ*, adorned with white garments, and blazing with the radiance of garlands of flames.
One should offer oblations there according to the prescribed rite as is appropriate;
having thus visualized the tongues of fire within the sacrificial fire, one should display one's own mudrā.
Forming the añjali with both hands, one should expand them into the shape of a lotus.
Oṃ kamalābhe svāhā.
This is the mudrā-mantra.
The middle finger raised specifically for every [other] finger shall be the Heart Mudrā of Agni; its mantra is also now being told.
Oṃ kuru 2 sva svāhā.
This is the heart-mudrā mantra of Agni.

Having grasped two *kuśa* blades that are neither too short nor too long, one should place them in the directions starting from the east; then, facing eastward, one should place them in the intermediate directions as well.
The ritual placement of the auspicious syllables (kuśanyāsa).
Having assumed that form of fire according to the distinctions of his respective functions,
the Supreme Lord holds a sacrificial pit, a lotus, a staff, a rosary, and a garland for recitation.
The glorious one, with a short and protruding belly, adorned with four arms,
shines with white and other colors according to the distinctions of the rites for peace and so forth.
His body is filled with the peaceful and other aesthetic moods (rasas), adorned with garments and ornaments;
his excellent upper body is further embellished by what is known as the ornament of the massed matted locks.
Having thus beheld the vajra-fire endowed with meditative cultivation,
one should likewise draw the gnosis-being from the sky into that heart.
Having caused [him] to enter by means of mantras, mudrās, and so forth, one should then speak these words:
"Come, come, O great being, O best of divine sages and twice-born!"
"Having accepted this oblation, indeed, be present here.
[With these words, one performs] the offering of water for honor (*argha*), water for the feet (*pādya*), the rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*), the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), and so forth.
Having offered the vessel and the *sruva* ladle, along with an oblation filled with clarified butter,
and having propitiated [the deity], one should, being firm and composed, speak this mantra:
Oṃ, to Agni, who has been kindled, enter, enter; for the glory of the covenant, O consumer of oblations, O carrier of oblations, accept this water offering, svāhā!
Then, one should offer two blades of dūrvā grass smeared with oil into the fire.
Oṃ vajrapuṣpe svāhā.
Of ghee: [Oṃ] Svāhā to Agni!
Oṃ, to the vajra that burns all sins, burn all sin, svāhā! Of sesame seeds:
Oṃ, to Vajrapuṣṭi, svāhā! Of unbroken white rice grains:
Oṃ mraṃ svāhā. This is for the curd-rice.
Oṃ vajrabījāya svāhā. For grains.
Oṃ, svāhā to the one of great speed; [this is] for barley grains.
Oṃ, svāhā to Mahābala! [This is for] the black gram beans.
Oṃ vajraghasmare svāhā | [This is] for wheat.
Oṃ apratihatavajrāya svāhā | [This is for] the kuśa grasses.
Oṃ vajrayajñāya svāhā. [This is] for the *audumbara* tree.
Oṃ, svāhā to the Bodhi tree; [this is] for the Aśvattha.
Oṃ vajralatāya svāhā | [This is for] the Plakṣa tree.
Oṃ vajrakuverāya svāhā. [This is] for the Nyagrodha tree.
Oṃ, to the mango tree, svāhā! [This is] for the mango.
Alternatively, having recited the mantras over campaka, aśoka, puṃnāga, kadambaka, or arjuna flowers as they may be obtained, one should perform the fire offering with them.
One should offer as oblations fruits such as grapes, palāśa, dates, and coconuts, according to one's availability, following the sequence of the ritual for the five wheels.
Through the five nectars, the five meats, and the meditations on the five maṇḍalas,
the mantra-practitioner is satisfied by the gratification of the fire of gnosis.
Then, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and having worshipped with garlands, sandalwood, and garments,
the Fire-god is likewise satisfied by those offerings.
Then, within the center of the hearth, the skillful practitioner should meditate upon the maṇḍala of his own chosen deity,
according to the specific ritual action, through the yoga of the moon, vajra, and so forth.
Having prepared the arghya, pādya, and other offerings as before, one should present them according to the prescribed rite;
one should offer three oblations for each of all the sacrificial substances.
Then, at the door of the mouth with the Vajra-tongue, one should offer water for rinsing the mouth;
next, one should give water for the feet at the feet, and especially flowers upon the head.
One should likewise offer incense before the radiance,
and having worshipped with flowers and other offerings, sandalwood should be applied to the head.
Having filled the *pātṛ* ladles with clarified butter and taken them up with the great *sruva* ladle,
the wise one should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) through union with his chosen deity.
Oṃ, to the fire of all Buddhas, svāhā!
Resembling the Śrīvatsa, the chowrie, the banner, the flag, the parasol, and the lotus;
known as the bell, the sword, and the trident; resembling the coils of a serpent at play.
Resembling the morning sun, with the luster of a svastika and Indra’s bow,
it is smooth like a right-spiraling conch and resembles coral and gold.
It possesses the brilliant, pure, and stainless luster of safflower, silver, and lapis lazuli;
it is smokeless, fragrant, and has the supreme sound of flutes and drums.
A fire with a single flame is the best and is praised for rites of pacification and the like;
one with two flames is declared middling, and one with three flames is indeed inferior.
It is smoky, inauspicious, of dull activity, with its crest and luster severed;
it is coarse, resembling black palāśa leaves, and looks like a thick mass of gośīrṣa resin.
Sparks and a harsh sound, and the scent of a cremation ground may arise;
by these aforementioned inauspicious omens, both Rakṣā and Kuṇḍalī are indicated.
The exposition of the characteristics of fire.
Now, however, the recitation of mantras for rites such as pacification (śāntika) is described:
one should employ the word "svāhā" in pacification, while the syllable "oṃ" is prescribed for prosperity (pauṣṭika).
The syllable *phaṭ* is used in malevolent rites (*abhicāra*); the syllable *jaḥ* is considered for summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*);
the syllable *baṃ* is renowned for binding; and the syllable *hūṃ* is considered for protection (*rakṣaṇa*).
The syllable *hūṃ* is known for slaying; the syllable *śrīṃ* for attracting wealth;
the syllable *hoḥ* for propitiation; and the syllable *bhrūṃ* is remembered for threatening.
The syllable *hiṃ* is used for selection; *hrīḥ* is the maker of universal forms. *Aṃ* is for warding off food;
*āḥ* is for invisibility; and *haḥ* is for accomplishment and immersion.

The intellect is for the accomplishment of the mandala, and the syllable HŪṂ is for making known the Dharma; having interlaced those seed-syllables according to the specific ritual action, one should proceed from there.
The preceptor should perform the fire offering constantly; thereby the Wielders of the Thunderbolt are pleased.
For the Eternal Victor, possessing the luster of molten gold, is satisfied.
The Jinas were pleased, as was Padmanarteśvara; the Lord of the best of horses was pleased,
as were Brahmā, Śakra, Maheśa, Viṣṇu, and the mighty Vāyu.
Kāmadeva, Halī, as well as the Moon, the Sun, and the planets; Pṛthvī, the wielder of the noose (Varuṇa), Cakravaira, and likewise Kuṇapa.
The King of Dharma, the nāgas, the gandharvas, asuras, and kiṃnaras;
the gods dwelling in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven and those residing in Akaniṣṭha.
Those who dwell among the Great Kings, those who abide in the Heaven of Others' Emanations, the gods who Delight in Creation, and those who have reached the Pure Abodes;
Those who dwell in the world-system of Mārīcī, those who inhabit the great realms,
the beings residing in the four continents, and those who abide within the three worlds.
The receptacle worlds consist of the realms of sentient beings, such as creepers, shrubs, and grasses;
as well as those who abide on the stage of Joy and those who have reached the further shore on the stage of Purity.
Those who dwell in Arciṣmatī and have made their abode on the mountain,
those who abide in Dharmameghā, and those who reside in Durjaya;
Those who have attained the stage of Dūraṅgamā and dwell in the Prabhākārī stage—
the lords of the ten bhūmis, the protectors, the noble eight great persons— [are present].
The Buddhas and the Śrāvakas, as well as those with the form of the rhinoceros-like Pratyekabuddhas,
along with the hungry ghosts, hell-beings, animals, gods, asuras, and humans.
Likewise, in the circle of the Gaṇas, one should constantly and unweariedly behold the deities whose nature is the body of Brahmā, pleased by the performance of the fire-sacrifice (homa).
Then, having performed worship with flowers and other offerings, and having again sounded the bell,
one should recite the hundred-syllable mantra and dismiss the fire-oblation once more.
